paragraphs.heading: The middle band of the Earth
paragraphs.text: Temperate climates belong to Earth's middle latitudes, roughly 23.5° to 66.5° north or south of the Equator, between the tropics and the polar regions. In the north the zone runs from the Tropic of Cancer up to the Arctic Circle. In the south it runs from the Tropic of Capricorn down to the Antarctic Circle.

paragraphs.heading: Wider swings, many controls
paragraphs.text: Compared with the tropics, temperate places usually swing through a wider range of temperatures in a year and have clearer seasons. Tropical seasons often differ mainly in how much rain falls. Latitude is not the only control. Sea currents, the direction of the prevailing wind, continentality (how big the landmass is) and altitude all shape a temperate climate too.

paragraphs.heading: Drawing the line with Köppen
paragraphs.text: In the Köppen climate classification, a climate counts as temperate, letter C, when its coldest month averages above −3 °C but below 18 °C, a limit meant to reflect lasting frost. Some versions of the scheme set the lower limit at 0 °C instead. A broader definition can also take in continental climates, letter D, which are more extreme, with the coldest month usually below −3 °C.

paragraphs.heading: The warm side
paragraphs.text: Some schemes split the zone into smaller ones based on monthly temperatures, the coldest month and rainfall. The subtropical part, between about 23.5° and 35°, feels the tropics most: summers are longer and hotter, winters shorter and milder, and freezing precipitation is uncommon. It holds two climates. Humid subtropical places have long, hot, humid summers with frequent showers and the most rain in the hottest months. Mediterranean places do the reverse, with dry summers and wet winters.

paragraphs.heading: The cool side
paragraphs.text: The cool temperate part lies between about 35° and 66.5° and also has two types, a milder oceanic one and a harsher continental one. Oceanic climates come from cool ocean air flowing ashore from the west. That gives mild summers, cool but not cold winters, and rain spread through the year, often under cloudy skies. Continental climates are made by large landmasses and winds that change direction with the seasons, so they swing between a hot summer and a cold winter.

paragraphs.heading: Where to find each one
paragraphs.text: Real places show the pattern. Coastal California, central Chile and the Western Cape of South Africa have Mediterranean climates. Northwestern Europe and most of New Zealand are oceanic. Southeastern Canada, Japan and the Korean Peninsula are humid continental.
